q-vulg-fiat-lux: The words are Genesis 1:3. Fīat is a subjunctive of the irregular verb fierī, 'let it become'; lūx, lūcis is a third-declension noun. The phrase later became the motto of several universities, including the University of California.
q-vulg-in-principio: The verse is John 1:1. Verbum translates the Greek logos, 'word, reason'. Erat, 'was', is the imperfect of sum. The Book of Kells and the Lindisfarne Gospels both decorate this opening.
r-vulg-john-1-5: Read it aloud twice: erat, verbum, deus and lūx come back again and again. Recognising repeated words in a real text is how reading fluency builds.
r-vulg-genesis-1-5: Monks chanted Genesis during the night office in the weeks before Lent, so these lines were heard every year.
q-gesta-latro: Augustine used the story to argue that a kingdom without justice is just a large band of robbers. The pirate's point is that the only difference between him and Alexander is scale.
q-hildegard-aurora: Hildegard (1098–1179) founded a convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen and wrote about 77 chants, along with books on visions and medicine. Pope Benedict XVI made her a Doctor of the Church in 2012.
q-colophon-tres-digiti: A colophon is a scribe's note at the end of a book. Writing by hand with a quill, often in cold rooms, was hard physical work. Trēs digitī, 'three fingers', is the subject; scrībunt is plural.
q-aug-tolle-lege: He tells the story in Confessions 8.12. The passage he read was Romans 13:13–14. Tolle and lege are imperatives of tollere, 'pick up', and legere, 'read'. He became bishop of Hippo in North Africa in 395 or 396.
q-bede-discere: The words come from the short autobiography Bede added at the end of his Ecclesiastical History, finished in 731. Discere, docēre and scrībere are infinitives used as nouns.
q-alcuin-epitaph: Alcuin of York (c. 735–804) ran Charlemagne's palace school at Aachen and later became abbot of St Martin's at Tours. Ancient tombstones often addressed passers-by in the same 'what you are, I was' way.
q-vulg-gloria: The words are Luke 2:14. In excelsīs means 'in the highest (places)'. The longer Gloria hymn was sung at Mass on Sundays and feast days.
q-vulg-pater-noster: The prayer is Matthew 6:9–13. Noster, 'our', agrees with pater; quī es in caelīs is a relative clause, 'who are in the heavens'. Sanctificētur is a passive subjunctive: 'may it be made holy'.
q-dies-irae: The hymn is usually attributed to the 13th-century Franciscan Thomas of Celano. Its rhymed three-line stanzas show how medieval Latin poetry used stress and rhyme rather than classical vowel length.
q-magna-carta-39: Nūllus liber homo means 'no free man'; in 1215 most English people were unfree peasants, so the clause first protected barons and freemen. Its idea of the lawful judgment of one's peers later shaped the US Bill of Rights.
q-bede-angli: Bede wrote the story in his Ecclesiastical History (2.1). Gregory became pope in 590 and sent Augustine, later the first archbishop of Canterbury, to Kent in 597. The pun works because Anglī and angelī differ by one letter.
q-aug-inquietum: Augustine wrote the Confessions as a long prayer addressed to God, telling the story of his youth and conversion. Fēcistī is the perfect of facere, 'you made'; dōnec, 'until', introduces the time clause.
q-vulg-per-speculum: The verse is 1 Corinthians 13:12, in Paul's chapter on love. Ancient mirrors were polished metal and gave a dim image. In aenigmate means 'in a riddle', from the Greek word that gives English 'enigma'.
q-ben-hospites: Benedict wrote that guests should be received 'as Christ', tamquam Christus, so monasteries took in travellers, pilgrims and the poor. The line is from Rule chapter 53.
q-ben-otiositas: The line opens Rule chapter 48, on daily manual labour. Benedict of Nursia wrote the Rule around 530–540, probably at Monte Cassino. Inimīca, 'enemy', is a feminine adjective agreeing with ōtiōsitās.
q-aug-sero: The prayer is Confessions 10.27. Augustine plays on time: the beauty is 'so ancient and so new', and he loved it 'late'. Sērō is an adverb; amāvī is the perfect of amō.
q-aug-da-mihi: The line is Confessions 8.7. Augustine admits he feared that God would grant his prayer too quickly. Dā is the imperative of dare, 'give'; nōndum means 'not yet'.
q-aquinas-tardiloquum: Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) taught at Paris and Naples and wrote the Summa Theologiae. The letter, De modo studendi, gives sixteen pieces of advice on study; its authorship is not certain.
q-archpoet-taberna: The poem is the Archpoet's 'Confession', also preserved in the Carmina Burana. Its stressed, rhymed lines are typical of medieval student poetry. Mihi est prōpositum, 'it is my plan', uses the dative of possession.
q-ben-ausculta: Auscultā is an imperative, 'listen', and the Rule begins with this call to attentive hearing. Benedictine communities around the world still read the Rule aloud daily.
q-vulg-de-profundis: The words open Psalm 130 (129 in the Vulgate numbering). Clāmāvī is the perfect of clāmāre, 'to cry out'. Dē profundīs means 'out of the depths'.
q-paris-statute-1215: Christian scholars were wary of Aristotle's ideas on the eternity of the world and the soul. By 1255 the Paris arts faculty required his works, and Aquinas and others built Christian thought around them.
q-ag-dei: The words echo John the Baptist in John 1:29. Agnus is second declension, 'lamb'; tollis, 'you take away', is the same verb as in Augustine's tolle, lege. The chant is repeated three times.
q-carmina-o-fortuna: The manuscript, now in Munich, holds over 250 poems in Latin and German, on love, drinking, gambling and satire. Orff's setting of O Fortuna is one of the most played pieces of classical music.
q-abelard-dubitando: Peter Abelard (1079–1142) was the most famous teacher in Paris. His method of setting out questions and conflicting answers became standard in medieval universities. Dubitandō is a gerund: 'by doubting'.
q-vulg-vanitas: The words open Ecclesiastes (1:2). Vānitās means 'emptiness'; the repeated genitive, vānitātum, is a Hebrew way of saying 'utter emptiness'.
q-kempis-transit: Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a canon in the Low Countries. The Imitation of Christ was printed in many editions and translated into many languages. Transit is the present of trānsīre, 'to pass over'.
q-heloise-meretrix: Héloïse (d. 1164) was one of the most learned women of her time; her letters with Abelard were written after both had entered religious life. Their Latin is full of Cicero and the classical authors.
q-boethius-rota: Boethius, a Roman senator, was imprisoned by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. The Consolation of Philosophy, written in alternating prose and verse, was translated by King Alfred and by Chaucer.
q-mon-unum: Dante (1265–1321) wrote De monarchia probably around 1312–1318; the Church later placed it on its list of banned books. Here he argues that peace needs one ruler, as one heart rules the body.
q-bede-sparrow: In Bede's story (Ecclesiastical History 2.13, set in 627) the counsellor argues that if Christianity tells them more about what comes before and after life, they should accept it. Edwin was baptised at York.
